title: A narrow margin
paragraphs: City governments now compete for skilled residents the way firms once competed for customers. The advent of remote work did not empty offices, but it did make the difference between cities easier to discern. A resident who can work from anywhere will not stay for a logo. What holds people is a distinct mix of rent, schools and a sense of esteem.

Officials are prone to allege that a new campus or a tax cut will accelerate growth. The estimates rarely survive contact with the housing market. Where the margin between wages and rent is already thin, a severe shortage of small flats matters more than another slogan. An effective initiative is usually dull: it suspends a rule that blocks small homes, then checks whether competent builders actually show up.

Optimistic forecasts still transform press conferences. They seldom transform a lease. Cities that prevail are the ones that can indicate, in numbers rather than adjectives, that an ordinary household can remain.

title: After the dry season
paragraphs: A long drought does more than soak the news cycle. It cuts acreage, dries moisture out of the soil, and leaves farmers accustomed to planning a year ahead with only a few weeks of certainty. Haste in this setting is expensive. A federal grant can leverage private credit, but it cannot compensate for a staple crop that never came up.

The shortage is no longer an anonymous rural phenomenon. Towns that overlook the disposal of failed harvests soon feel an intense pressure on prices. The incentive to recruit seasonal labour weakens once farms cannot pay. Some workers leave; others stay and watch a tendency harden into a habit: plant less, insure more, and hope the next season is not as dry.
Public money still arrives. What it rarely does is arrive before the decision to abandon a field has already been made.
